Q: `reinterpret_cast` between unrelated structs A:

This is undefined behavior in standard C++, even if all your static_assert pass.

Your checks only prove that the two types have the same size, alignment and memory layout but the C++ object model is stricter than just same size + same layout.

According standard, an object can only be accessed throught its own type.

On your code, A and B are diffferent and unrelated types.

So, accessing an object of type A throught a B* pointer breaks the strict aliasing rule.

Q: Is the brute-force "Balanced Binary Tree" solution really O(n^2) with early exit? A:

First, note that nlogn is still O(n^2), so technically there is nothing wrong with what the link says. I do think you are correct though in saying its O(nlogn). Also note this was asked here: https://cs.stackexchange.com/questions/165123/time-complexity-determining-if-a-binary-tree-is-balanced (but a satisfactory answer is not provided).

Let r be the root and let the tree have n elements. You first compute the heights of both the left and right subtrees, which effectively visit all the vertices in the tree. So you do O(n) work. If your balancing condition is met, you recurse on both left and right subtrees; otherwise, you stop and say unbalanced. So you always do more work when your balancing condition is met. Taking out the root, there are n-1 elements left. No matter whether n is even or odd, if balanced, the size of each sub-tree is at most (n+1)/2.

Repeating the same argument as for the root, you get the recurrence: T(n) <= O(n) + 2.T((n+1)/2). For simplicity, take the constant in big-O to be 1. So, T(n) <= n + 2T((n+1)/2).
Maybe you know a better way, but if you just expand the recurrence, you get that the total time spent is upper-bounded by n + 2.(n+1)/2 + 4.(n+3)/4 + 8.(n+7)/8 ......

There can be at most say t = logn + 10 terms, because after that your parameter would be (n+2^{t-1})/2^t <= 1/2^9 + 1/2 < 1. So total work is O(nlogn) + 1+3+7+15+... (Mersenne numbers, t terms), where being generous, the last sum can be bounded by say 2^{t+5} = 2^{logn + 15} = O(n). Thus total work is O(nlogn).
